title: Can UNH's Focus on Special Needs Plans Strengthen Medicare Growth? - The Globe and Mail
content: UnitedHealth Group IncorporatedUNH is refining its Medicare Advantage strategy, emphasizing high-value health maintenance organization (HMO) plans and specialized coverage for seniors with complex healthcare needs. For 2027, UnitedHealthcare plans to prioritize Chronic Special Needs Plans (C-SNPs) and Dual Eligible Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs). The opportunity is substantial. UnitedHealthcare's C-SNPs will be available to nearly 50 million Medicare-eligible individuals in 2027, offering tailored support for people managing conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic heart failure. Meanwhile, its D-SNPs will reach approximately 74% of dual-eligible individuals, facilitating coordinated Medicare and Medicaid benefits. These plans can connect members with more coordinated care, medication support and preventive services, potentially creating opportunities to improve outcomes and limit avoidable healthcare spending. UNH's approach also fits its broader shift toward more selective Medicare Advantage offerings. The company is adjusting plan benefits and market participation to better align coverage with healthcare costs. It expects Medicare margins to approach the upper end of its 2%-4% target range in 2026, reflecting improved cost management and product positioning. Integrated care through Optum Health could further support this strategy by coordinating services for members with complex needs. Star ratings remain another consideration. UnitedHealthcare reported that at least 69% of its Medicare Advantage members are in plans rated four stars or higher for 2027. UNH's focus on special needs plans could support targeted growth, but execution, medical costs and quality performance can shape the results. Some of UNH’s major competitors in the healthcare service provider space are Humana Inc.HUM and Centene CorporationCNC. Humana is expanding its Chronic Condition Special Needs Plans into Pennsylvania, Utah and Wisconsin for 2027. HUM’s focus on tailored coverage and coordinated care could attract beneficiaries with complex conditions, while stronger Star Ratings may support its Medicare Advantage competitiveness. Through its Wellcare brand, Centene is emphasizing affordable Medicare Advantage coverage and integrated care for dual-eligible beneficiaries in 2027. CNC’s coordinated Medicare-Medicaid offerings could strengthen its appeal among members with complex needs, although managing medical expenses remains key. Shares of UNH have gained 19.5% in the year-to-date period compared with the industry’s rise of 22.9%. title: What Happened With UnitedHealth Stock This Week? - Trefis
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group (UNH) rose 4.5% over the two trading days through Wednesday, October 14, while the S&P 500 fell 1.1%. The company reported fiscal Q3 2026 results before the market opened on Tuesday. The stock slipped 0.2% that day before posting its gain on Wednesday. Management also raised its forecast for full-year 2026 earnings. So what did the report change for someone who owns the shares? Fiscal Q3 2026 earnings per share came in at $4.69, clearing the $4.18 analysts expected. Revenue matched estimates almost exactly at $113 billion. The surprise was in profit, not sales. On Tuesday, the market treated the report as little news. The S&P 500 was nearly flat. UnitedHealth moved alongside CVS Health and Cigna, which also edged lower, while Elevance Health rose. How Far Has UnitedHealth’s Profit Margin Come Back? Through fiscal Q2 2026, UnitedHealth’s operating margin, the share of revenue left after the costs of running the business, returned above its level a year earlier. The margin was 4.6% in fiscal Q2 2025. It fell to 3.8% in fiscal Q3 2025 and 0.3% in fiscal Q4 2025. This margin decline occurred during a year of growing sales. In FY2025, UnitedHealthcare, the largest segment, grew revenue 15.7%, and Optum Rx grew 16.1%. The margin then recovered to 8.0% in fiscal Q1 2026 and 7.1% in fiscal Q2 2026. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue grew only 0.4%, so the extra profit came from keeping more of each dollar rather than selling more. On a twelve-month view, profit has not come back. Diluted earnings per share were $15.54 in the twelve months to June 2026, down from $23.08 a year earlier. Management now expects more from 2026 than it did three months ago. On October 13, the company raised its full-year 2026 forecast for GAAP diluted earnings per share to at least $19.50, up from $18.70 in July. A forecast is not a result. How Did UnitedHealth Explain Its Third-Quarter Results? Management credited the quarter to discipline and execution across every part of the business. The next report, covering the fourth quarter, is expected on or around January 25, 2027. Full-year 2026 diluted earnings per share, measured against management’s raised forecast of $19.50, is the number to watch in that report. Now you know UNH better. title: UnitedHealth Beats on Earnings, But Investors Question Growth Path - MarketBeat
content:
For the third consecutive quarter, UnitedHealth Group NYSE: UNH delivered a beat on both its top and bottom lines. But, as with the company’s Q2 2026 report, investors gave the news a lukewarm response. UNH shares opened about 5% higher and touched $399.88. By mid-afternoon, they had given back all their gains and slipped below their 50-day moving average. UNH is down sharply since reaching a 52-week high in July. The earnings report showed that UnitedHealth Group’s turnaround is going well. But with the easy comps in the past, investors are wondering where the growth will come from. In Q3 2026, revenue came in at $112.7 billion, topping expectations, but it was slightly below the $113.2 billion UNH reported a year ago. That decline is by design, and it’s central to understanding this quarter. UNH is shedding members and markets that don’t meet its profit targets. On the earnings front, the news was even better. This was the fourth consecutive quarter in which UnitedHealth beat expectations for adjusted earnings per share (EPS). Adjusted EPS of $4.69 jumped 61% year over year (YOY). The company also raised its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to at least $20.50, a 25% YOY increase. But the headline results from the earnings report require context. That context helps explain the lukewarm post-earnings reaction. If investors want to understand UnitedHealth’s Q3 earnings report, they should pay close attention to this statement from CEO Stephen Hemsley: “Our third quarter results reflect the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business, as we continue evolving UnitedHealth Group to deliver a simpler, more supportive experience for patients and the clinicians who care for them.” In practice, simpler means smaller. UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people at the end of September, down from 50.1 million a year earlier. Much of this is deliberate. Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, and risk-based commercial membership each fell about 10%. UNH closed more than 100 Medicare Advantage plans for 2026, covering about 600,000 members. Others left after facing higher costs or thinner benefits. The payoff shows up in the margins. The medical care ratio, the share of premiums spent on care, fell to 88.4% from 89.9%. UnitedHealthcare’s operating margin rose to 3.3% from 2.1%. Optum Health’s margin climbed to 3.2% from just 0.2%, even as its revenue fell 10%. One caveat: the quarter included $610 million of favorable reserve development, worth roughly 0.7 points on that ratio. The dividend is an attractive selling point for UNH. The yield of 2.4% isn’t particularly impressive. However, it pays $9.28 per share annually, which is an attractive payout for income-seeking investors. Cash flow supports that payout. Operating cash flow reached $25.1 billion through nine months, up from $18.6 billion a year ago. It also explains why the stock has rallied hard since closing at a low of around $257 in late March. Healthcare has been a logical choice for investors looking for alternatives outside the technology/AI trade. At 19x forward earnings, UNH also trades at a nice value compared to its history and the broader market. But a long-term buy-and-hold investment requires some growth, and getting a bit smaller and more selective doesn’t count as growth. At least it doesn’t count in a sustainable way. Revenue is up just 0.6% through nine months. And the shrinkage isn’t finished. About 390,000 members are in plans to be discontinued for 2027. Bulls have a fair counterpoint. Margin recovery alone could lift 2027 earnings. The question is how much recovery remains. Investors may get a clearer answer in January, when UNH typically issues its outlook for the year ahead. Still, UnitedHealth remains one of the best names in the healthcare sector. The 12-month growth in UNH is a testament to that. This may be a case where investors weren’t wrong, just early. If that’s true, the consensus price target of $462.59, which implies about 18% upside, looks very attractive. But there may be some bumps along the way. Those bumps are already visible on the chart. Since July, UNH has made lower highs and lower lows. The rising 200-day moving average at $358 is the key support. A move above $400 would challenge the downtrend. A break below $365 would confirm it. Volume is worth watching in the days ahead, since it shows how much conviction sits behind the selling. title: CNC, UNH, CVS, HUM Stocks Slip After-Hours — Trump Administration Reportedly Seeks To Scrap Subsidies On Certain Medicare Plans - Stocktwits
content: Shares of health insurance companies, including Centene (CNC), slipped after-hours on Tuesday following a report that the Trump administration plans to end a federal subsidy program that has helped suppress Medicare Part D prescription drug plan premiums. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. The Journal states that about 25 million Americans are enrolled in Part D plans, with the average monthly premium this year running near $36. The Wall Street Journal reports the decision could leave many seniors confronting higher premiums for their stand-alone prescription coverage beginning in 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. Loss of the $3.6-billion in support could pressure margins if insurers absorb costs or reduce competitiveness through higher premiums, risking enrollment declines. However, beneficiaries might also migrate to Medicare Advantage plans and help offset losses. Centene holds the largest share of stand-alone Medicare Part D (PDP) enrollment via Wellcare — more than eight million members as of early 2026, or about one-third of the entire PDP market, exceeding the exposure of its rivals. CNC shares dived 3% after hours on Tuesday, while shares of UNH, CVS, and HUM fell by about or less than 1%. In a major bid to accelerate American dominance in the commercial space sector, the Trump administration announced a proposal allowing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to bypass lengthy environmental reviews for rocket launches, spacecraft reentries, and commercial launch site approvals. The initiative, announced on Tuesday by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, aims to eliminate red tape for commercial operators as the U.S. prepares for an unprecedented surge in orbital launches and space infrastructure development. Commercial space stocks, including Rocket Lab (RKLB), AST SpaceMobile (ASTS), Intuitive Machines (LUNR), and Planet Labs (PL) dropped between 3% and 7% on Tuesday, while SpaceX (SPCX) added 3%. Under the proposed framework, the FAA would gain the authority to waive requirements established across 13 major federal environmental statutes. These include the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Clean Air Act. Federal officials emphasized that exemptions would only apply where environmental rules delay innovation, maintaining that core public health, national security, and safety safeguards will remain intact. "America won the first Space Race, and we can do it again -- but only if we get government red tape out of the way," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated, noting that the goal is to lower costs and strengthen U.S. competitiveness. Environmental assessments—which currently can take over a year to complete—have long been a target of frustration for commercial launch providers. While conservation groups view these evaluations as crucial for protecting coastal wildlife habitats, launch companies have repeatedly slammed the reviews as duplicative administrative bottlenecks. The FAA's proposal opens a 30-day public comment window before final rules are enacted. The drive to deregulate comes as the commercial space industry experiences exponential growth. The FAA reported authorizing a record 204 commercial space operations in FY2025. Much of this growth is being driven by heavyweights like Elon Musk’s SpaceX, Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, and rising startups like Stoke Space. These firms are aggressively deploying satellite constellations for broadband connectivity, defense applications, and orbital data centers.                         Kirsteen Mackay UnitedHealth raised its 2026 earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per adjusted share as third quarter results showed a lower medical care ratio and more profit. UnitedHealth's third quarter showed its cost controls are taking hold, as a lower medical care ratio helped lift operating earnings and supported a higher 2026 outlook. Gains came across UnitedHealthcare and Optum despite falling membership. Management sees 2027 growth near the low end of its long-term target, though medical costs, Medicaid funding and federal legal actions remain risks. UnitedHealth Group Inc. (NYSE: UNH) on October 13, 2026, raised its full year 2026 earnings outlook and now expects adjusted net earnings of at least $20.50 per share. The company said the forecast incorporates its experience through the third quarter 2026. On a GAAP basis, UnitedHealth now expects full year earnings of at least $19.50 per share. GAAP refers to standard US accounting rules, while the adjusted figure excludes items such as the amortization of acquired intangible assets and gains or losses tied to business sales. The updated outlook follows third quarter adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, compared with $2.92 in the third quarter 2025. GAAP diluted earnings were $4.56 per share, up from $2.59 a year earlier. The release lists the Department of Justice's legal actions concerning UnitedHealth's participation in the Medicare program among the factors that could cause results to differ from expectations. It also cites changes in Medicare, the CMS star ratings program and risk adjustment data validation audits, which review the diagnosis data used to set government payments. UnitedHealth's medical care ratio, the share of premium revenue spent on patient care, was 88.4% in the third quarter, compared with 89.9% a year earlier. The company attributed the decline to medical cost management, benefit design changes and pricing. The ratio included $610 million of net favorable prior period reserve development related to 2026 dates of service. This means UnitedHealth's earlier estimates of claims owed for care delivered this year proved higher than the amounts now expected. Earnings from operations were $6.6 billion, compared with $4.3 billion in the third quarter 2025. The company said the increase was driven by execution across both its UnitedHealthcare insurance unit and its Optum health services unit. Consolidated revenue was $112.7 billion, compared with $113.2 billion a year earlier. Revenue in the second quarter 2026 was $112 billion. The operating cost ratio, which measures administrative costs against revenue, was 12.8%, compared with 13.5% in the third quarter 2025. The company said efficiency gains were partly offset by increased spending on technology, processes and staff. "Our third quarter results reflect the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business," Stephen Hemsley, Chief Executive Officer, UnitedHealth Group, said in the earnings release. UnitedHealthcare earned $2.8 billion from operations in the quarter, up from $1.8 billion a year earlier, on revenue of $86.3 billion. The unit served 48.3 million people, compared with about 50.1 million at the end of the third quarter 2025. The number of seniors served through Medicare Advantage, including programs for complex populations also covered by Medicaid, has contracted by 935,000 since year-end 2025, according to the release. Optum Health revenue fell 10% to $22.9 billion. The company said it served fewer patients under value-based care, arrangements in which providers are paid based on patient outcomes and costs, in markets where it lacked enough presence to sustain its clinicians. Optum Health earnings from operations rose to $735 million from $41 million a year earlier. The company attributed the change to operational discipline and medical cost management in its value-based care markets. Optum Rx, the company's pharmacy benefits business, reported earnings from operations of $1.7 billion, compared with $1.5 billion a year earlier. Adjusted scripts fell to 393 million from 414 million, which the company linked to membership declines at UnitedHealthcare and other customers. Optum Insight, the data and technology unit, reported revenue of $5.5 billion, up 3% from a year earlier. Its earnings from operations rose to $1.3 billion from $920 million. On the earnings call, Tim Noel, who leads UnitedHealthcare, said commercial medical cost trends are running above the company's initial expectation of 11%. He cited costs tied to the No Surprises Act dispute process, greater cost intensity from clinicians and high-cost specialty drugs. The No Surprises Act is a federal law intended to protect patients from unexpected medical bills. Noel said arbitration awards under its dispute process can approach nearly 6% of total medical spending in some regions. Noel said UnitedHealth continues to view 2026 as a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which it now expects to be moderately better than negative 1%. He said the main variable remains the timing and adequacy of state funding. UnitedHealth's debt-to-capital ratio was 41.7% as of September 30, 2026, compared with 41.2% at the end of the second quarter. The company said it continues to target approximately 40% by year-end. The company repurchased $5 billion of its stock and paid $6.2 billion in dividends through the first nine months of 2026. Chief Financial Officer Wayne DeVeydt said the company expects dividends to exceed $8 billion by year-end. Management said it views the lower end of its 13% to 16% long-term growth target as a more reasonable starting point for 2027 and plans a fuller update in December, though elevated medical cost trends, government program funding and the Department of Justice's legal actions remain key risks to that outlook. Shares of the iPhone maker clocked an all-time high of $334.68 on Thursday amid a series of positive catalysts for the company. China's cyberspace regulator on Wednesday approved the registration of Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones in the country, clearing a key regulatory hurdle for the long-awaited launch of Apple's AI features in the country. Under Chinese rules, companies must obtain approval for large language models and generative AI services before releasing them to the public. Apple Intelligence is expected to leverage AI models from Baidu and Alibaba. Meanwhile, HSBC upgraded AAPL stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold,’ with a price target of $366, implying an upside of 10% from the stock’s last close. Apple has drawn increased attention in recent weeks after it announced hikes in prices for several products, including MacBooks, iPads, HomePods and Apple TV devices, fueling speculation that iPhone price increases could follow. Investors are also focused on the company's upcoming leadership change, with John Ternus set to succeed Tim Cook as CEO on Sept. 1. AAPL stock has risen nearly 23% so far in 2026, while retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing. Eli Lilly said that it will acquire all outstanding ATAI shares for $6.75 per share in cash, with shareholders eligible for an additional up to $2.50 per share if certain development and regulatory milestones are achieved, bringing the deal's total potential value to $9.25 per share. The cash offer represents a 25.9% premium to ATAI's Wednesday closing price, while the maximum consideration implies a 72.6% premium. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) suffered their worst one-day drop in more than two years on Thursday after a $1 billion convertible-note raise rattled investors, but options veteran Jon Najarian said that the deal still represents “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” ASTS stock plunged 17% on Thursday to close at $55.01, marking its lowest closing level of the year. Najarian and his brother Pete Najarian broke down the financing and ASTS’ selloff in a Market Rebellion video posted on X. The brothers co-founded Market Rebellion, an options-focused market analysis platform, in 2016. AST SpaceMobile priced $1 billion of 1.625% convertible senior notes due in 2034, with an initial conversion price of $79.57 per share, which was about 20% above Wednesday’s close. Jon Najarian said that the notes give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to convert into ASTS shares at that price. While the 1.625% coupon is relatively low, he said the real appeal lies in the potential equity upside. “If the stock’s 200 bucks, you’re still exercising it at $79.57,” he said, calling the structure “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” The $200 figure was a hypothetical example, not a formal price target. Pete Najarian said that investors were focused on the risk that the notes could eventually convert into shares and dilute existing holders. “They’re concerned about dilution and all the rest of it,” he said, adding that the stock’s negative reaction was “understandable.” Still, he agreed the financing could support a valuable long-term opportunity. “I think this could be something into the future that could be pretty special, quite frankly,” he said. The brothers also stressed that ASTS remains a highly volatile trade. Implied volatility in the options was around 100%, according to Pete Najarian. “The implied volatility of this thing is not a joke,” he said. “Hell yes, this thing is volatile.” AST SpaceMobile said proceeds remaining after capped-call transactions may be used to secure additional access to orbit through “partnerships and/or acquisitions.” The company said the move could further vertically integrate its business and reduce reliance on third-party launch providers, although it currently has no agreement for any transaction. Satellite communications analyst Tim Farrar said that the language pointed to a potential acquisition. Potential names raised included United Launch Alliance, Firefly Aerospace, Relativity Space and Stoke Space. Farrar also said that AST may be trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertically integrated model across launch and satellite infrastructure. “ASTS were outbid for Iridium, so it looks like they are now trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertical integration play,” he said. The Najarians also suggested acquisitions may be part of the plan. “They’ve got some ideas with partnerships, acquisitions, all that kind of thing that people are excited about,” Jon Najarian said. “They just needed the capital,” he added. The financing comes as AST SpaceMobile continues expanding its BlueBird satellite network. BlueBird 10 recently deployed its communications array in low Earth orbit, while BlueBirds 8 and 9 are next. BlueBird 11 has arrived at Cape Canaveral, and BlueBirds 12 and 13 are being transported from Texas to Florida. AST said that the newer satellites are expected to deliver nearly twice the peak speeds of its first-generation spacecraft. title: UNH secures homecoming victory over Elon - The New Hampshire
content: October 3rd, 2026 marked the University of New Hampshire’s (UNH) 99th Homecoming Football Game, and the precedent was celebrated in style. The Wildcats (‘Cats) took home an impressive victory over Elon, winning 30-23 at Wildcat Stadium. Leading up to the much-anticipated homecoming match, seas of UNH students, alumni, family and friends poured into Boulder Field and A-lot. With Durham overflowing with spirit, and Wildcat stadium sold out, the ‘Cats did not disappoint. The first ‘Cats possession ended after 5 plays and a punt. This punt was bobbled by Elon’s returner, and picked up by ‘Cats receiver #17 Logan Perez. He brought the ball down to Elon’s 1-yard line, and the ‘Cats capitalized early in the first quarter with a 1-yard rushing touchdown from #11 Barry Kleinpeter. After the extra point was knocked in by #99 Logan Glassburn, the ‘Cats led by 7. Two possessions later, the ‘Cats marched down to the Elon 10-yard line, before having to settle for 3 points, the field goal was knocked in by Glassburn, 10-0 Wildcats. Elon answered with a field goal of their own, moving the score to 10-3. The final scoring act of the first quarter was claimed by UNH, as Logan Glassburn knocked in another field goal, giving the ‘Cats a 13-3 lead at the end of the first quarter. The ‘Cats conceded an early touchdown during Elon’s first drive of the second quarter,with the made extra point kick moving the score to 13-10. Elon’s quarterback threw a pair of interceptions to ‘Cats safeties in the second quarter: one to #12 Jackson Stone and the other to #10 Cohen Cook. UNH marched down the field on the final drive of the half, and Glassburn knocked in another field goal, moving the ‘Cats lead to 16-10. The ‘Cats first offensive possession of the second half yielded a 27-yard touchdown pass. UNH Quarterback #7 Brooks Bently threw a ball just short of the endzone to the open man #24 Joquez Smith, who turned and freely ran into the endzone. The extra point knocked in by Glassburn resulted in a 23-10 UNH lead. Elon answered with a touchdown of their own on the next possession, then promptly with a field goal, cutting the UNH lead down to 3, 23-20. The first drive of the 4th quarter for the ‘Cats yields a big pass from Bentley, caught by #88 Drew Danson, in the endzone for a UNH touchdown. Glassburn knocked in the extra point, and UNH led 30-23. Elon’s final score of the game came from a field goal, cutting the ‘Cats lead down to 4, 30-26. But it was too little, too late, and the ‘Cats took home the Homecoming victory. This week, the Wildcats take on Monmouth at Wildcat Stadium on October 17th, 2026.

At the same time, demand has gradually improved, providing an additional tailwind for companies across the sector as they prepare to report Q2 results. The rally highlights growing investor confidence in Penguin's expanding role in enterprise artificial intelligence infrastructure, as demand for high-performance computing and memory solutions remains strong. Penguin Solutions posted its strongest-ever Q3 results, with revenue rising 48% year-on-year to $479 million and earnings of $0.84 per share, exceeding the analysts’ consensus estimates of $421 million and $0.56 per share, respectively, according to Fiscal AI data. title: UNH sees nearly 5% bump in enrollment; new students getting record financial aid - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: The University of New Hampshire welcomed 3,000 new students to its Durham and Manchester campuses this fall, representing a nearly 5% increase from last year’s incoming class. The university said the uptick in new students is bucking national trends. First-year undergraduate students at UNH increased 3.5% and transfer students increased 11.2%, compared with 2025 enrollment numbers. Other numbers from UNH about this fall’s new class: Out-of-state enrollment grew 11%, while in-state enrollment grew 1.7%. UNH said these figures reflect its “strengthened position in the New Hampshire market.” “While there are many challenges facing higher education right now, by focusing on a high-quality academic experience, experiential learning, and creating value for students and their families, we are increasingly a first-choice for many,” UNH President Elizabeth Chilton said in a news release Tuesday. Earlier this month, the University System of New Hampshire announced it would begin offering free tuition at the state’s public colleges to certain students beginning next year. Eligible students must be New Hampshire residents, meet certain academic requirements and be attending one of the schools for the first time. Their families cannot earn more than $100,000 a year. A UNH spokesperson estimated the change in eligibility requirements will mean an additional 29% of next year’s incoming class will qualify for the program. NHPR is nonprofit and independent. title: UNH Stock Outpaces S&P 500 In 2026, Eyes Best Year Since Pandemic — CFO Says Wall Street May Be Missing 2027 Upside - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth (UNH) have outpaced the S&P 500 so far in 2026 and are on pace for their strongest year since 2021. Now, CFO Wayne DeVeydt says Wall Street may be underestimating the company’s earnings opportunity in 2027. UNH stock is up nearly 17% in 2026, outpacing the S&P 500’s 14% gain and the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund’s (XLV) 11% rise. The rebound follows a 33% plunge last year. UnitedHealth reported third-quarter (Q3) adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, topping the $4.14 analyst consensus. Revenue also beat estimates, coming in at $112.69 billion on $111.49 billion, though it was slightly below the $113.2 billion reported a year earlier. Earnings from operations climbed to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion. The company raised its 2026 adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share, from a previous range of $19.50 to $20. But even after its recent rebound, UNH shares are up just 19% since January 2021, a 3% annualized gain over nearly six years. “Current analyst consensus for 2027 may understate the opportunity ahead,” DeVeydt said on the earnings call. He added, “The quality of earnings is strong and durable as we head into 2027.” He called the lower end of UnitedHealth’s long-term adjusted earnings growth target of 13% to 16% a “reasonable starting point.” By Stocktwits’ calculation, 13% growth on the $20.50 floor would imply about $23.17 a share in 2027. Analysts’ quarterly estimates compiled by Fiscal.ai sum to about $22.80. DeVeydt cited share repurchases, value-based care, enterprise-wide progress and gains from artificial intelligence and modernization as potential tailwinds. He also flagged policy reforms, modernization spending, medical-cost trends and pressure on health-benefit funding as headwinds. Quarterly revenue climbed 61% from $70.2 billion in the first quarter of 2021 to $112.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Operating profit, however, was nearly unchanged, slipping from $6.7 billion to $6.6 billion. Revenue hovered around $112 billion in the second and third quarters of 2026, while earnings per share swung more sharply. Basic EPS fell to nearly zero in the fourth quarter of 2025, rebounded to $6.90 in the first quarter of 2026, then declined to $6.10 in the second quarter and $4.60 in the third. UnitedHealth reported adjusted EPS of $2.11 for the fourth quarter of 2025. Analysts estimate basic EPS will peak at $8.20 in the first quarter of 2027, then fall to $6.90 in the second quarter, $4.80 in the third and $2.90 in the fourth, according to Fiscal.ai. UnitedHealth’s average 12-month analyst price target is $480.68, implying about 27% upside from current levels. Of 26 analysts, 7 rate the stock ‘Strong Buy,’ 15 ‘Buy’ and 4 ‘Hold’; none rate it ‘Sell’ or ‘Strong Sell,’ according to Koyfin. UnitedHealth’s medical care ratio fell to 88.4% in the third quarter from 89.9% a year earlier, reflecting tighter pricing, benefit changes and cost controls. The result also included $610 million in favorable reserve development. But the ratio rose from 86.7% in the second quarter, and commercial medical trends remained above 11%. When asked whether the trends were worsening, UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said, “We are not seeing the dynamics that you are talking about.” Medicaid is another pressure point. UnitedHealth expects 2026 to be a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which it now projects to be moderately better than negative 1%. The firm expects margins to return to targeted levels by the end of 2028. At least 69% of UnitedHealthcare’s Medicare Advantage members are in plans rated four stars or higher in the 2027 star ratings, which affect bonus payments in 2028. The company expects that share to reach 75% as it moves through 2027 and into 2028, compared with a 70% industry average. The company plans to focus on high-value Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) plans and special-needs plans for people with chronic conditions or who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. UnitedHealthcare is UnitedHealth’s revenue heavyweight, bringing in $86.3 billion in the third quarter. It provides health coverage to employers and individuals and runs the company’s Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans. Revenue dipped from $87.1 billion a year earlier, but operating earnings climbed to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion. Optum is the group’s health-services engine. Optum Health delivers care and manages provider networks. Optum Rx handles pharmacy services and prescription benefits. Optum Insight provides tech and data services to healthcare organizations. Together, the businesses generated $66.9 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in operating earnings. Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) climbed nearly 1% overnight late Tuesday after an executive said that the company is planning 12 hypersonic test launches this year, spotlighting its role in the U.S. push to develop advanced weapons faster. RKLB stock fell 2% on Tuesday to $64.22, logging its fifth straight session in the red. Rocket Lab’s vice president of global launch services Brian Rogers said that said HASTE enables “low cost, high frequency hypersonic and missile defense testing.” Short for Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron, HASTE is a suborbital test-launch vehicle derived from Rocket Lab’s Electron rocket. It carries experimental payloads for flight testing. Rocket Lab says it can carry payloads of up to 700 kilograms and release them at speeds above 7.5 kilometers per second. The company reported a 100% success rate across HASTE flights in March. “Rather than saying we need to be stuck in an analysis environment and then it’s a very rigorous test campaign that costs a lot of money and involves a lot of people, now you can say we’re planning 12 tests this year,” Rogers told Fox News. “We don’t have to bet the farm on any one of them, which allows us to take more risk and really move the needle in terms of technology development.” The U.S. military is replenishing its missile stockpile, while developing hypersonic weapons, but the systems are costly. Government Accountability Office estimates put the Army’s Dark Eagle missile at more than $40 million each. A Navy estimate for a hypersonic missile planned for Zumwalt destroyers is about $70 million, including development and integration costs. By comparison, a Tomahawk costs about $2.6 million and an Army Precision Strike Missile about $1.6 million. Some startups are targeting lower prices. Castelion says its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon will cost less than $500,000 and is designed for mass production. Rocket Lab has secured a series of contracts for hypersonic testing. In March, it signed a $190 million deal for 20 HASTE flights over four years under the MACH-TB 2.0 program. Anduril followed in May with a $30 million contract for three HASTE test launches. In July, Rocket Lab announced a $266 million Space Force contract for 12 suborbital launches, with options for six more. The missions will primarily launch from a new site in Kodiak, Alaska, with the first expected no earlier than the end of 2026. Rocket Lab said the award will provide high-frequency launch capacity for missile-defense missions. Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the UnitedHealth Group third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. A question and answer session will follow UnitedHealth Group's prepared remarks. As a reminder, this call is being recorded. Here is some important introductory information. This call contains forward-looking statements under U.S. federal securities laws. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from historical experience or present expectations. A description of some of the risks and uncertainties can be found in the reports that we file with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including the cautionary statements included in our current and periodic filings. This call will also reference non-GAAP amounts. A reconciliation of the non-GAAP to GAAP amounts is available on the financial and earnings reports section of the company's investor relations page at www.unitedhealthgroup.com. Information presented on this call is contained in the earnings release we issued this morning and in our Form 8-K, dated October 13, 2026, which may be accessed from the investor relations page of the company's website. I will now turn the conference over to Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of UnitedHealth Group, Steve Hemsley. Steve Hemsley: Good morning, and thank you for joining us today. Our third quarter performance reflects actions taken throughout 2026, driving meaningful progress and reinforcing our confidence to sustainably grow in 2027 and beyond within our 13%-16% long-term target growth range. Our revised full year 2026 guidance reflects continuing improvements in leadership and execution across Optum and UnitedHealthcare as we better align our businesses to serve the demands of the ever-changing U.S. healthcare environment. We are accelerating the modernization of our enterprise by advancing simplified and more responsive policies, processes, and tools, focusing on more effective integrated value-based care offerings, and responsibly building modern agentic infrastructure as we seek to ensure people have access to higher quality care at lower costs, and at the same time, clinicians experience a simpler, faster, and more supportive system. Across the businesses, AI-enabled capabilities are beginning to help clinicians spend more time with patients, improve service speed and experience, streamline administration, and reduce friction for both consumers and clinicians. A few examples. We have expanded AI-enabled chart summarization to more than 40% of our employed clinicians, reducing chart review time by 33%. AI-enabled information gathering and research have shortened appeal cycle times by 26%, improving both member and clinician experience, and we expect this to accelerate in 2027. For this year's Medicare Advantage annual enrollment period, we are introducing AI-powered plan recommendation that use a member's care history and local plan options to help simplify their selection. By the end of this year, we are on track to implement all previously announced prior authorization reforms, reducing decision timelines for patients, relieving administrative burden for clinicians, and delivering better experiences for people. Collectively, these initiatives will reduce total prior authorizations by 30%, including a reduction of two-thirds in prior authorizations for people under the age 18. These efforts are only the beginning. More will follow. They are central to how we're changing our enterprise to be more in line with our mission, creating greater value and positive social impact. In that vein, an important effort is the reimagined United Health Foundation. With $1 billion committed to date, the foundation's investments, along with the dedicated operational expertise of UnitedHealthcare and Optum, can help facilitate scaled solutions to some of the U.S. health system's greatest challenges, including rural health, maternal and infant health, behavioral health, and workforce education. As just one example, in Tennessee, the foundation is helping expand and operate health hubs across the state, providing access to underserved communities in preventative care and chronic condition support. We will continue to highlight the foundation as part of our commentary on our earnings calls going forward. The broader healthcare environment remains dynamic. Policy-driven regulatory developments, changing consumer expectations, and the rapid evolution of clinical care and advances in technology continue to reshape the industry. These factors are pressuring basic affordability and access as never before. Success requires continuous adaptation, and the pace is accelerating. We recognize this and remain restless in our pursuit of change and improvement. We are challenging our assumptions, revising policies and practices, and repositioning leadership and capabilities to better meet the needs of those we serve and to move faster as an enterprise to adapt to the changing healthcare landscape. That includes opportunities to better align with clinical partners, employers, government benefit sponsors to help improve the experience of all stakeholders in healthcare. We've made progress in our 2026 performance. We have much to do to approach the full potential of our mission and the positive impact we can make as an enterprise. UnitedHealth Group has a long history of evolution to meet the needs of a changing U.S. health system. We're committed to accelerating these efforts as a stronger, more capable, more mission-centered enterprise. With that, let me turn the call over to Tim Noel. Tim Noel: Thanks, Steve. UnitedHealthcare is seeing positive momentum across our Medicare and Medicaid businesses. While our commercial business continues to adjust to a challenging but steadily stabilizing environment. Costs remain stubbornly high across the entire healthcare landscape, and particularly in areas such as specialty pharmacy and acute healthcare service intensity. We continue to address the challenge of increasingly expensive care with appropriate medical management, operational discipline, and a commitment to identify and remove excess and unnecessary costs from our own enterprise as we advance simpler and more modern services. We are working to deliver stable benefits and value for our members and customers. We believe this positions us for continued organic growth and long-term value creation entering 2027. Let me start with our Medicare business, where the annual enrollment period begins later this week. Medicare Advantage remains the choice of well more than half of eligible American seniors as it offers better and more modern benefits, and importantly, better outcomes than fee-for-service Medicare. Beneficiaries choosing Medicare Advantage save on average more than $4,000 annually through lower premiums and cost sharing than those on original Medicare. With adequate funding, we believe Medicare Advantage will continue to be the choice of American seniors, particularly those who are disadvantaged and have chronic care challenges as they seek better value and modern care. Heading into 2026, we made deliberate decisions regarding Medicare Advantage benefit design and market positioning to preserve the long-term sustainability and performance of our Medicare Advantage offerings. We continued this disciplined approach for 2027. We believe we are competitively positioned, focused on providing value for seniors in the markets we serve while being mindful of trend dynamics. In 2027, UnitedHealthcare will continue to prioritize high-value HMO, chronic special needs, and dual special needs offerings. Our commitment to serving America's seniors is clear. More than 94% of Medicare-eligible individuals nationwide will have access to a UnitedHealthcare Medicare plan, and approximately 90% of Medicare-eligible consumers will have access to one of our Medicare Advantage plans with a $0 premium option. We are maintaining important benefits such as dental, vision, hearing, and additional health and wellness offerings that make a real difference in the lives of seniors. UnitedHealthcare chronic special needs plans will be available to nearly 50 million Medicare-eligible individuals in 2027, providing specialized support for people living with conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and chronic heart failure. These plans offer benefits and access to care tailored to the unique needs of individuals managing chronic conditions, helping them connect with care, medications, and support they need. Much of this work is in coordination with our partners at Optum Health, where evidence shows chronically complex seniors served by integrated value-based care experience better preventative care while improving health outcomes at lower costs. Medicare Advantage patients in value-based care arrangements are 40% likely than traditional Medicare patients to be hospitalized for acute and chronic conditions, and 40% less likely to be readmitted to a hospital within 30 days of discharge. Moving to Stars. Our initial Star Ratings for payment year 2028 reflect our investment in quality, member experience, and operating execution. As we move through 2027 and into 2028, we expect to approach 75% of total members in four-plus Star plans compared to the industry average of 70%. Our team remains intensely focused on building a best-in-class consumer and clinical experience. Along with better benefit design and stability going forward, we believe those efforts will continue translating into stronger quality performance over time. We will continue to work in support of the CMS quality program efforts to ensure the Medicare Advantage program continues to provide quality experience and stability to the 36 million seniors who depend on it. Turning to medical costs. The actions we've taken to improve and modernize care management, strengthen clinical engagement, and enhance operating discipline are having a meaningful effect. Care intensity remains elevated relative to historical norms, even as we continue to see signs that trends are bending in a more stable direction than what we have recently experienced. We remain respectful of trends, and are not assuming any deceleration to historical patterns or to ongoing clinician pricing pressure. Demand for care remains strong, particularly among senior and complex populations, and we fully support appropriate access to care for our members. Turning to the commercial business. Performance continues to stabilize as we navigate a challenging market. As we previously noted, trends for commercial benefits are exceeding our initial expectations of 11%, driven by an acceleration of costs related to the No Surprises Act, greater cost intensity from clinicians, and high-cost specialty drugs. Of particular concern is the ongoing abuse of the No Surprises Act dispute process by a relatively small number of clinician groups and third-party organizations. Arbitration awards can approach nearly 6% of total medical spend in some regions, translating to billions of dollars in excess costs for consumers, employers, and the health system. The law was intended to protect patients from unexpected bills, and we strongly support that objective. We will continue working with policymakers and regulators to ensure the law functions as intended and that healthcare dollars are directed towards appropriate patient care rather than significantly inflated market arbitration awards and volumes, along with unnecessary administrative expense. Medicaid remains stable through the back half of the year, while our team continues to drive greater operational improvements through network curation and more effective behavioral health program initiatives. These actions help to partially offset the primary variable, which continues to be the timing and adequacy of state funding across several markets. As we move through the balance of 2026, we continue to work collaboratively with our state partners to ensure rates appropriately reflect the acuity and healthcare needs of the families being served, including the impacts of regulatory actions. While progress has been made in many states, the timing of updates remains uneven. Based on our current outlook, we continue to view 2026 as a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which we now expect to be moderately better than negative 1%. Finally, we are focusing intensely on enhancing our support for, and relationships with, clinicians and health systems. In addition to the prior authorization changes Steve mentioned, which we see as only the beginning, we are meaningfully speeding up our claims processing and payments, and re-energizing our relationship engagement efforts with more dedicated resources and executive ownership. Our goal is to provide a more seamless experience for clinicians and health systems who work with us and to resolve issues more quickly. As we look towards 2027 and beyond, we are shifting our focus to sustainable organic growth underpinned by improving Medicare fundamentals, a stronger commercial outlook, continued opportunities to enhance Medicaid performance, and an organization that is operating with greater discipline and accountability for all our stakeholders. With that, I'll turn it over to Patrick. Patrick Conway: Thanks, Tim. Our results from the third quarter underscore the important work underway across all of Optum to lay the groundwork for long-term growth. Starting with Optum Health. Overall, Optum Health continued to deliver strong performance in the third quarter, driven by the continued return to value-based care principles, combined with strong execution across our clinical programs and operational improvements, enabling clinicians to focus more on their patients and improve patient experience. A few of the examples for this morning, a 27% increase from last year in online self-scheduling, making it easier for patients to reach clinicians. An increase in home health visits by 10% over last year. We are very encouraged by the early success of our program to co-locate behavioral specialists within our primary care practices. The number of patients referred has doubled since last year, with an engagement rate of more than 90%. As Tim mentioned, it is now more important than ever to provide seamless care and coverage for our chronic and complex patients through all phases of the care continuum, from primary care to specialist, to home to the pharmacy. Moving to Optum Rx. Our focus in this business continues to be on two efforts to ensure value alignment to the customers and patients we serve. First, we continue to increase transparency on the PBM side of Optum Rx. Through the 2027 selling season, we have seen our industry-first affordability, experience, and transparency initiatives resonating in the marketplace and customers. The employers, governments, unions we serve continuing to recognize the vital role of PBMs in controlling prescription drug costs and ensuring people have access to the medications they need, particularly as the prices charged by drug manufacturers continue to increase. For the first time, over 50% of Optum Rx membership is external, non-UHC membership. Second, we fundamentally believe that pharmacy services have to be closer to the patient. Accordingly, you will see continued efforts within our separate pharmacy services businesses to more closely align pharmacy care with medical care. Integrated value-based care means just that, integrated. When pharmacy care and medical care are aligned, outcomes improve for the patients we serve, access improves, and the total cost of care is lowered. Specifically, within the pharmacy service side of Optum Rx, Genoa continues to expand its dedicated behavioral health pharmacy footprint and serve patients with serious mental illness and substance use disorders. Specialty pharmacy continues to grow through both volume and mix while improving patient support for increasingly complex therapies. Infusion services are becoming more important as we help shift appropriate care into lower cost and more convenient settings. We will continue to expand our portfolio of integrated pharmacy services and align them as close to medical care settings as possible, delivering better care, convenience, and access. Turning to Optum Insight. 2026 has been both a performance and an investment year, and 2027 will show meaningful progress, setting the foundation for accelerating growth in 2028 and beyond. Our investment focus has been on further developing and bringing to market healthcare-specific AI solutions that enhance productivity performance outcomes while improving the patient and clinician experience. Overall, we are looking to 2027 with confidence. Our major remediation work is largely complete, and it's created a strong foundation for growth across Optum. With that, I'll turn it over to Wayne. Wayne DeVeydt: Thanks, Patrick, and good morning. Third quarter results reflect continued progress across the enterprise and improving execution in our businesses where we have been focused on operating reforms to drive better consumer and clinician experience. For Q3 2026, we reported revenue of $113 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $4.69, up from $2.92 a year ago. Consolidated medical care ratio of 88.4% for the quarter compares to 89.9% last year. The quality of earnings is strong and durable as we head into 2027. At UnitedHealthcare, performance continued to reflect pricing discipline, fundamental medical cost management, and care delivery enhancements. We continue to be respectful of continued elevated utilization trends, which typically step up in the back half of the year, particularly in our risk-based businesses. Within Optum Health, we are seeing steady progress from modernization, a return to a disciplined value-based care approach, and operating improvements as the actions taken through 2026 begin to yield results. In Optum Insight, performance is benefiting from technology and AI-enabled improvements, including payment integrity and broader operating efficiency while we invest into the new areas to expand and modernize our offerings to drive growth. In Optum Rx, we continue to see the benefits of disciplined execution and the breadth of our pharmacy services model now based on a simpler, more transparent approach to serving these evolving market needs. Turning to the full year, our updated 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of at least $20.50 reflects performance through the third quarter, balanced by expected investments in the final months of the year. From a capital deployment perspective, our priorities remain consistent. First, reinvest in the business through targeted organic growth and steady expansion in care delivery, technology, modernization, and broad-based AI adoption. Second, maintain balance sheet strength. Third, return value to shareholders. Our balance sheet remains strong. Our debt-to-cap ratio was 41.7% at the close of the quarter, and we remain on track to approach 40% by year-end. We repurchased $5 billion of UNH stock through the third quarter. We have paid $6.2 billion in dividends year to date and expect to exceed $8 billion by year-end. Our strategic priorities remain focused on capabilities that align with and strengthen our ability to deliver value to consumers, benefit sponsors, and customers and support long-term growth for shareholders. We view our 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of at least $20.50 as a solid run rate on which to grow. The University of New Hampshire is welcoming a 5 percent increase in first-year students this semester, defying national higher education trends. UNH says the Class of 2030 represents the strongest academic profile in UNH history and includes an 11 percent spike in out-of-state enrollment, drawing students from 40 states and 25 countries. "We have worked really hard to communicate the message of value to our prospective students," said Kim DeRego, the vice provost for enrollment management at UNH. Value means not only cost, but internships and job placement. DeRego noted that roughly two-thirds of undergraduates complete an internship during their time at the university. "It leads to over 95% job placement rate when they leave campus," she said. The university's substantial growth stands out against modest gains seen across the country. Data from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center indicates that undergraduate college enrollment grew by just 1 percent nationwide in 2025. Students on campus point to specialized, accelerated academic pathways as a primary reason for choosing the university. Emmalee Coombs, an incoming student from Pelham, said she selected the school specifically for its accelerated career track. "I was drawn to UNH because I am in the occupational therapy program," Coombs said. "I was interested in this because of the five-year program and being able to graduate with a master's in five years, and the opportunities that come with it straight out of school." Other students highlighted unique structural degree paths. "I am doing the 2-plus-2, so I get my vet tech after two years, and then I get my bachelor's degree after four years," said Aryanna Cardillo. title: PSC organizes vigil to honor victims in Gaza - The New Hampshire
content: On Wednesday Oct. 7, the Palestine Solidarity Coalition (PSC) organized a vigil on the Great Lawn at the University of New Hampshire (UNH) to honor the victims of the ongoing war in Gaza, recognizing it as a genocide against the Palestinian people. Oct. 7 2026 marks 3 years since the war began in 2023, however the conflict between Israel and the Middle East had begun around a century earlier. When Israel declared independence in 1948, it went to war with five Arab nations. It is important to note, tensions had been growing even before 1948. Emory Stevens, UNH senior and lead organizer of PSC began the ceremony with a speech. Stevens highlighted shocking facts about the war including 175,000 Palestinians being injured or killed, and 1.9 million people displaced since 2023. Stevens also called Israel’s ceasefire a “facade”, considering the 325 attacks by Israel in the last 600 days. “How are they allowed to target hospitals and schools?” said Stevens. Stevens recognized that standing against Israel on the UNH campus is radical due to the funds the university receives from Israeli organizations. UNH receives 0.5% of their $475 million endowment from Israeli organizations. Stevens held a moment of silence for the victims, asking that the participants think of one tragedy from the war that made an impact on them. “It’s important to make Palestine visible to all palettes of life,” said Stevens in an interview. Around 20 people participated in this event, in which Stevens opened the floor for anyone to speak. Two representative members from the Southern New Hampshire Young Democratic Socialists of America (SNHYDSA) Patience Corbett and Kevin Boardman were in attendance. SNHYDSA is currently petitioning on campus to stop UNH from receiving funds from Israel. The organization had received 50 signatures as of Wednesday, and they do not plan on slowing down. Along with these efforts, they are looking to open a chapter at UNH. Boardman is concerned about Israel and the U.S.'s relationship and how Israel could influence the state of our country. “American police officers go to Israel to learn tactics,” said Boardman. Boardman encouraged everyone to spread the message by talking to two friends or family members that might not know about this cause. PSC says they will continue their efforts to support Palestinian people by raising money for their annual May Day for Palestine event; the date is TBD.

title: The “Protect College Sports Act”: What it means for UNH athletics - The New Hampshire
content: On Sept. 28th, the Protect College Sports Act was passed by the U.S. Senate in a sweeping win of 77-22, and is headed to the House of Representatives. The bill, introduced in June, will instate federal rule to help safeguard college athletes rights, regulate Name Image Likeness (NIL) compensation, retain fair competition, and stabilize the environment of college athletics. It attempts to create a semblance of control through the chaos that comes with collegiate level sports. Senator from New Hampshire, Maggie Hassan, is in support of the act. “Unfortunately, we have seen too many college athletes not benefit from their own success, or worse, see their plans for the future derailed by an injury,” said Hassan. Holding the schools to a national standard supports students who decide to move from one school to another, no longer changing rules they were previously accustomed to. The act prohibits schools and the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) from blocking athletes' pay. There are guidelines for NIL; any deal over $600 needs to be reported to the school, the deals have to be real business deals and not through other universities or colleges to transfer or enroll, and NIL agents must register with a state and can only take up to 5% of an endorsement deal. “Predatory agents cannot take advantage of student athletes and [the new NIL guideline] guarantees scholarships for 10 years so that students can finish their degrees regardless of what happens on the field,” said Hassan. Professor Michael McCann is the Associate Dean for Academic Administration & Intellectual Life and Founding Director of the Sports and Entertainment Law Institute at UNH. He explains that the effects of the bill on UNH versus larger Division I (D1) schools is similar as it helps stabilize our rosters. However, the effects can largely differ when we look at other specific additions, such as the new retention pool of $22.5 million with an additional $5 million for women athletes and non-revenue sports. This adds to the existing revenue-sharing amount of $21.5 million adding up to $49 million. “The vast majority of Division I schools, including UNH, seem unlikely to choose to spend anywhere near the max amount,” said McCann. “I imagine that spending discretion would primarily be used by power conference programs, such as colleges in the Southeastern Conference.” One of the strongest protections towards athletes in the bill requires D1 schools to pay for sports-related medical costs for 5 years post eligibility. This applies to injury treatment, second opinions, and catastrophic injury insurance. “Schools can make enormous profits from athletics programs, so it’s important that the student athletes who make these profits possible aren’t left behind,” said Hassan. Many athletes can suffer when playing sports, possibly ending their career. Having this support from their university or college can help make sure they are still able to pursue a successful future. Transfer rules now apply so that each athlete gets one free transfer without losing eligibility; after that, an athlete may have to sit out a year—unless extenuating circumstances apply. This rule aims to settle the constantly changing rosters and makes the system more predictable. Something similar has been applied to the coaches, wherein they can not participate in another team’s season before that team’s season has ended or their own prior team’s season has ended - whichever happens last. Another part of the bill protects Olympic and non-revenue sports. It states that big schools must keep the same number of roster spots and scholarships for non-revenue sports as they had in 2024-2025. This rule lasts 9 years and is designed to stop cutting programs such as swimming, track, gymnastics, and more. However, the topic of passing through the House brings up the question of whether it will run out of time before the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3rd. The amendments that have been proposed could also cause significant changes from what the Senate has passed. When it comes to how this federal rulebook could change recruiting techniques, UNH may have to switch tactics but not necessarily because of the bill passing. Professor McCann explained that whether or not the bill passes, recruiting strategies have always, and will always, continue to evolve. Not to mention as more high school athletes earn NILs, “the more conversant and knowledgeable recruiters are about NIL, the more they would have a leg up over competition.” The University of New Hampshire must continue to adapt to our changing media based world. New NIL rules may also change how athletes are persuaded to choose a school, with all funding and coercion from private parties being better monitored. Whether or not the bill passes, there are some major issues brought up that each university may decide to address. UNH may decide to adjust the budget, monitoring NILs, or taking on medical coverage from the passing of the bill, or because they believe in the changes that were proposed.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said financial bubble unwinds can get ugly depending on leverage, when asked what a potential unwinding of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade might look like. Speaking on Semafor's Compound Interest podcast, Goolsbee described a conditional scenario in which the fundamentals are not there and the AI trade proves to be a bubble. He noted that the U.S. has experienced bubbles before, including in the recent past, whose unwinds “can get ugly” depending on the leverage associated with them. Goolsbee said an AI unwind could resemble the experience with internet infrastructure investment. He recalled infrastructure being built around expectations of 20% annual growth, only for the growth rate to come in at 7% annually, which he described as still pretty strong. However, builders massively overbuilt, leaving an overhang. Goolsbee said the internet-era overbuilding, where growth fell short of expectations, was “slightly different” from an “old-fashioned bubble.” Asked about Former Fed Chair Alan Greenspan's view that the Fed could not deflate bubbles in real time without causing wider economic pain, Goolsbee said economists have a very significant debate about whether the Fed should prevent bubbles, pop them or clean up afterward. The Fed president also expressed increasing nervousness that AI investment was becoming a source of old-fashioned overheating demand. He cited conversations with Illinois businesses reporting difficulty finding electricians, elevated construction costs and one-year waiting lists for electrical components amid competition with data centers. Goolsbee distinguished between increased data-center activity at the expense of other sectors and overheating across the broader economy. He said AI had not overheated aggregate demand, but was starting to. Conditions were starting to feel like aggregate overheating, with AI data-center cost increases spreading beyond directly related industries, he said, warning that further increases spreading into general services would be problematic. Goolsbee said rates could come down if there is evidence that inflation is heading back toward 2% while maintaining full employment. However, he cautioned that rising services inflation and AI demand spreading beyond its own sector to overheat the broader economy could complicate that path. “The more you see services inflation going up and the more you see AI demand jumping out of its lane and overheating the rest of the economy, then it's going to be a little dicier,” he said. title: What is the Sustainability Dual Major at UNH? - University of New Hampshire
content: Sustainability dual majors study how environmental, social, and economic systems affect one another. Instead of treating challenges such as climate change, food insecurity, biodiversity loss, or social inequity as isolated issues, students learn to understand the relationships among them. Depending on their interests, students may explore topics related to natural resources, food systems, energy, business, public policy, environmental justice, or community resilience. They also develop skills in systems thinking, collaboration, communication, and problem-solving through projects and community-based experiences. Students can use their sustainability electives to explore questions related to their primary field. A student studying environmental conservation and sustainability might examine climate economics or natural resource policy. An agriculture and food systems student could focus on agroecology, food policy, or community resilience. A student majoring in marine, estuarine and freshwater biology might explore marine policy or sustainable fisheries, while a nutrition student could examine sustainable food systems. These different pathways allow students to bring a sustainability perspective to the subjects they already plan to study. Durga Raja ’25 paired the sustainability dual major with environmental and resource economics. She also participated in the climate action clinic, completed an internship with the UNH Sustainability Institute, and took part in two summer sustainability fellowships. “My favorite experience was being a student consultant in the Climate Action Clinic during my sophomore year, and then I served as a peer mentor for the next five semesters. I worked with local businesses and organizations to help measure their carbon footprints and support decarbonization efforts. That experience showed me how sustainability goals can look very different across sectors, while giving me the chance to collaborate with peers, work directly with clients, and make a real impact.” Students can apply what they learn through projects, internships, fellowships, and community partnerships. The required Sustainability Capstone is a community-based action-research experience. Students work in groups on a sustainability issue affecting UNH or the broader community. They present their work at the Undergraduate Research Conference, prepare a research paper, and create a professional portfolio. Students may also earn credit for practical work or a project through a sustainability internship. Additional opportunities offered through the UNH Sustainability Institute include paid internships and summer sustainability fellowships. Students from any major may also participate in programs such as the B Impact Clinic, where interdisciplinary teams work with regional companies assessing their social and environmental impacts. Availability and application requirements for these experiences may vary. The sustainability dual major at the University of New Hampshire is an interdisciplinary second major that students can combine with any four-year primary major. Through the program, students explore environmental, social, and economic challenges while learning how sustainability relates to their primary field of study. A dual major is an additional area of study completed alongside your primary major. At UNH, it has more requirements than a minor but fewer than a second or double major. To declare the sustainability dual major, students must have a primary major and a minimum GPA of 2.5. Students who have not yet chosen a primary major can still take the program’s introductory sustainability course to begin exploring the field. The dual major requires 32 credits, including three required courses and 20 credits of approved electives. Students select electives from both the natural or biological sciences and the social sciences or humanities, giving them opportunities to connect sustainability with their academic interests. Because the sustainability dual major is paired with a primary major, students can apply what they learn in a range of professions. UNH identifies potential career areas including corporate social responsibility, public relations and communications, nonprofit management, public policy and administration, social venture entrepreneurship, green engineering and design, community and urban planning, international development, and environmental or social science research. The program is designed to help students understand how their professional work can contribute to sustainable communities and how people from different disciplines can collaborate on complex challenges. The program may be a good fit if you want to connect your primary field with questions about human wellbeing, equity, natural systems, or long-term decision-making. It may also appeal to you if you enjoy examining problems from several perspectives and collaborating with people from different academic backgrounds. Explore the sustainability dual major at UNH to review current requirements, elective options, and experiential opportunities. You can also talk with your academic advisor about how the dual major could fit into your academic plan. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

UnitedHealth Group (NYSE: UNH) shares advanced following its October 13, 2026, earnings release as the largest U.S. private health insurer delivered stronger-than-expected third-quarter profits and raised its annual outlook for the third time this year. The stock traded around $383–$387 in early trading, compared with its October 12 closing price of $378.52. The results provided further evidence of a recovery after two years of elevated medical costs, restructuring and pressure on its Medicare Advantage business. Third-quarter revenue reached $112.69 bn, exceeding the $111.40 bn LSEG consensus, although it declined slightly from $113.16 bn a year earlier. Net income increased to $4.11 bn, or $4.56 per share, from $2.35 bn, or $2.59 per share, in the prior-year quarter. Adjusted EPS rose to $4.69 from $2.92, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s $4.14 estimate. Operating earnings increased to $6.6 bn from $4.3 bn, while operating cash flow reached $5.1 bn. The company now expects adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $20.50 per share, compared with its previous forecast of $19.50–$20. The most consequential development was a reduction in the medical care ratio to 88.4%, compared with 89.9% a year earlier and analysts’ expectations of 89.9%. The improvement reflects revised insurance pricing, benefit adjustments and efforts to manage healthcare utilization. It also benefited from $610 mn in favorable reserve development related to earlier 2026 medical services, a factor investors should distinguish from recurring cost savings. CFO Wayne DeVeydt cautioned that medical expenses remain elevated compared with historical levels. The federal independent dispute resolution process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least one percentage point to the company’s medical costs, according to DeVeydt. Hospital inpatient services and expensive specialty medications remain additional sources of pressure. UnitedHealthcare generated $86.3 bn in revenue and $2.8 bn in operating earnings. Membership declined to 48.3 mn, reflecting the company’s decision to reduce exposure to less profitable insurance contracts. Medicare Advantage membership has fallen by approximately 935,000 since the end of 2025. Optum reported $66.9 bn in revenue and $3.7 bn in operating earnings, supported by improved performance in clinical care operations. Management is also expanding value-based care arrangements and AI-assisted administrative tools. Acute hospital admissions declined 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions increased 10%. These changes may help reduce treatment costs, although their longer-term financial contribution remains dependent on execution. Wall Street analysts maintain a consensus Buy rating on UnitedHealth, with an average 12-month price target of $480.60 across 26 analysts surveyed by S&P Global Market Intelligence. Individual forecasts include UBS at $490, RBC Capital Markets at $478, Piper Sandler at $463 and TD Cowen at $402. The broader analyst target range extends from $380 to $529, reflecting differing assumptions about medical expenses, membership growth and the recovery in operating margins. UnitedHealth’s preliminary 2027 earnings outlook may be more significant than the quarterly earnings beat. DeVeydt suggested that earnings growth at the lower end of the company’s long-term 13%–16% objective represented a reasonable starting point for next year. Applying 13% growth to the updated 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $20.50 produces approximately $23.17 per share for 2027, above the existing Wall Street consensus of $22.61. At an early-session share price of approximately $384, UnitedHealth trades at about 18.7 times its minimum projected 2026 adjusted earnings and 16.6 times the illustrative 2027 figure. That valuation leaves room for appreciation if earnings recover as management anticipates. Risks remain substantial, including medical inflation, changes in Medicare Advantage reimbursement, declining membership and weaker quality ratings that could affect future bonus payments. For the next 12 months, analyst targets around $463–$490 imply approximately 21%–28% upside from $384, provided UnitedHealth continues improving profitability and delivers the earnings growth management has outlined. The third-quarter results support a more constructive earnings outlook, but the critical measure will be whether UnitedHealth can sustain lower medical cost ratios without relying heavily on favorable reserve adjustments or further reductions in membership.
