title: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs - CNBC
content:
UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook, as the company continues to manage high medical costs and sees investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold. The nation’s largest private insurer said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share. The healthcare giant’s turnaround plan is gaining momentum after three consecutive strong quarters this year. UnitedHealth is working to stabilize margins by shrinking membership, exiting unprofitable contracts, and ramping up investments in artificial intelligence and value-based care, which tie doctor and facility compensation to patient health outcomes, quality of care and cost effectiveness rather than the volume of medical services provided. “You’ll see in the quarter that we continue to execute not only on the financial aspects of our business, but really doing them with a simpler approach and an approach that’s really focused on investing heavily in value-based care,” CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview. Here’s what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: The company posted third-quarter net income of $4.11 billion, or $4.56 per share, compared with $2.35 billion, or $2.59 per share, in the same period a year ago. Excluding items like business divestitures, restructuring and the expected reduction of reserves for unprofitable contracts, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share. Revenue fell to $112.69 billion from $113.16 billion a year earlier. The company’s insurer, UnitedHealthcare, and its Optum healthcare unit both topped analysts’ operating earnings estimates for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Notably, UnitedHealth’s medical cost ratio — a measure of total medical expenses paid relative to premiums collected — came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. Analysts were expecting a ratio of 89.9%, according to StreetAccount. A lower ratio typically indicates the company collected more in premiums than it paid out in benefits, resulting in higher profitability. Still, DeVeydt told CNBC that medical costs in the quarter “continue to be elevated versus historical norms” — an issue that has plagued insurers, particularly those operating privately run Medicare Advantage plans, for more than two years. “I think it’s something we should keep an eye on. I think you’ll see that our medical care ratio has improved quite a bit, but I don’t want that to be misleading in terms of [medical cost trends],” DeVeydt said. He said the independent dispute resolution, or IDR, process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least 100 basis points, or 1 percentage point, to total medical costs. That federal law, which took effect in 2022, aims to protect consumers from unexpected medical bills. The IDR process allows providers and insurers to resolve disputes over out-of-network payments. DeVeydt said those changes are driving up the company’s claims costs, which can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher premiums. DeVeydt added that costs for inpatient services and pharmacy, particularly costly specialty pharmacy drugs for cancer and rare diseases, remain elevated. Still, he highlighted the company’s value-based care efforts, which he said are helping control medical costs by steering patients toward the right providers and emphasizing preventive care, DeVeydt added. He said acute hospital admissions among UnitedHealth members fell 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions rose 10%, suggesting more patients are receiving care in lower-cost settings. “You’re finding more members are actually getting into a lower-cost care environment, but more importantly, they’re getting into the care environment they actually want to be in,” he told CNBC. “So we think we’re really balancing both the quality and the cost.” UnitedHealth is also rolling out AI-powered ambient listening tools to reduce physicians’ administrative burden and free up time for patient visits. The trick is to get there.” Burry added that Puts account for about 10% of his portfolio. Long positions and LEAPS make up most of the rest, with minimal cash. “If the market crashes hard, I think I’ll do ok,” he said, adding that he expects his long holdings to perform over three to five years. “A year is nothing.” Burry’s reluctance to add shorts does not mean he has dropped his bearish bets. In his most recent Substack post, he said almost all his short exposure was expressed through puts on the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor stocks. The options expire in 2027 and were 20% out of the money. He put his window for a significant market top at zero to nine months. Burry sold his Fannie and Freddie common shares and added them to junior preferred stock (JPS). When asked how he moved from Fannie common into Freddie common and then out of both, he replied: “Almost as soon as I dumped the Fannie into Freddie, I was not comfortable with my risk position and started moving all and then some into the JPS.” The preferred shares rank above common stock in the capital structure. Burry’s thesis is that they could benefit if the government resolves its senior claims and reinstates preferred dividends. He said the junior preferreds could trade well above par depending on interest rates, adding that the potential return “from current levels” could reach four to five times. The main risk is the Treasury’s senior preferred stock liquidation preference, which Burry puts at about $388 billion, about twice the companies’ combined book value. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX) edged up on Monday even as Chinese memory-chip advances pressured sector stocks, with CEO Elon Musk weighing in on China’s manufacturing scale and calling SpaceX an “anomaly in the matrix.” SPCX stock rose 0.5% on Monday, marking its second straight gain after ending the previous week 2.3% higher. Micron fell 4% on Monday, while other memory and storage companies, including SK Hynix, Samsung, SanDisk, Seagate and Western Digital, also declined after Chinese chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) outlined plans for a new DDR5 server-memory product. CXMT said it aims to launch a server memory module using a “4F square” DRAM design by the end of the year. The architecture aims to pack more memory cells into the same chip area as the 6F square design widely used today, potentially increasing density. Musk contrasted China’s manufacturing scale on X with SpaceX’s launch lead. “When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined,” he said, citing lithium batteries and solar. He said SpaceX is a “rare counter-example”: it puts an order of magnitude more mass into orbit than the rest of the world, although China now accounts for most non-SpaceX mass to orbit. “SpaceX is an anomaly in the matrix,” he added. Musk then turned to memory chips, noting that RAM was a “low margin commodity” only about three years ago. He said LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 share a common standard that China “seems to be solving fast,” while newer high-bandwidth memory architectures, an SRAM layer beneath logic, 3D-stacked RAM above logic and the challenge of cooling the logic will be “harder to solve.” Musk’s comments follow SpaceX’s August earnings call, when he said memory supply was struggling to keep pace with AI-driven demand. He said memory output was growing about 20% a year while demand was increasing 200% or more, a gap he said could push prices higher. The supply issue matters to SpaceX’s expansion into AI computing, alongside its launch and Starlink businesses. Under a multi-year Google cloud-services agreement disclosed in June, Google is set to pay SpaceX $920 million a month from October 2026 through June 2029 for access to computing capacity, including about 110,000 Nvidia GPUs and related infrastructure with memory. The company reported $15.8 billion in AI-related capital expenditures, within about $18.4 billion in total capital expenditures. Revenue reached $7.8 billion, while SpaceX recorded a $541 million net loss. Musk is also pursuing a longer-term chip-supply strategy through Terafab, a Texas facility to make, package and test logic and memory chips. Intel joined the project in April, with its 14A manufacturing process expected to be used at the fab. In August, SpaceX and Tesla announced an initial $16.8 billion investment in the project. Musk also said recently that TSMC could potentially sublease part of the facility, while Tesla and SpaceX would retain ownership.
